chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim al-Hadrami, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, a man from the Ansar in the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) went out for one of his needs, so he made a pledge to his wife that she should not leave her house until he returns.

And her father fell ill, so the woman sent a message to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) saying, 'My husband went out and pledged to me that I should not leave my house until he returns, and my father has become ill, so order me to visit him.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'No, sit in your house and obey your husband.'
So he became seriously ill, so she sent to him a second time with that, saying, 'So if you order me, I can visit him.' So he said, 'Sit in your house and obey your husband.'
So her father died, and she sent to him, 'My father has died, so order me to pray over him.' So he said, 'No, sit in your house and obey your husband.'
So the man was buried, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sent to her, 'Indeed, Allah has forgiven you and your father due to your obedience to your husband.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a wife's obedience to her husband if it conflicts with visiting her parents?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *ta'ah* (obedience) to the husband, highlighting how the Prophet (peace be upon him) prioritized the marital covenant over filial duties, even in the face of the father's illness and death. Shia scholars often cite this to demonstrate that spousal obedience is a binding religious obligation, provided it does not involve sin, establishing a hierarchy of domestic responsibilities. The narrative concludes with divine reward, linking the woman's patience and compliance directly to the forgiveness of both herself and her father.
